analysis.one_liner: Extends children's online privacy protections to teens and bans targeted ads aimed at children and teens.
analysis.headline: A House subcommittee advanced the bill 14-10 on December 11, 2025, sending it to the full Energy and Commerce Committee; no floor vote has happened yet.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill updates a 1998 law that protects kids' privacy online. It would extend those protections to teens aged 13 to 16, ban companies from using children's and teens' personal data to target them with ads, limit what data companies can collect and how long they keep it, and give parents and teens the right to see, delete, and correct that data. It also requires clear notice and consent before collecting a child's or teen's information and restricts storing that information in certain foreign countries. [S2]
analysis.who_benefits: Parents of children under 13, and teens aged 13 to 16, gain the right to know what data companies hold about them, to have it deleted or corrected, and to stop it from being used for advertising. Families also gain protection against having kids' biometric and location data collected or sent to certain foreign countries without notice. [S2]

how_it_helps.text: The bill bans operators from collecting, using, or sharing a child's or teen's personal information for individual-specific advertising, including profiling based on demographics like age, sex, income, race, or ethnicity, or letting anyone else do so. [S2]

It extends the law's coverage from children under 13 to teens, defined as anyone over 12 and under 17, and requires operators to get verifiable consent before using or disclosing such information. [S2]
Teens and parents gain rights to see what personal information is held, delete it or content they posted, refuse further use, and correct inaccurate information. [S2]

It limits collection to what is consistent with the requested service, bars retaining data longer than reasonably necessary, and requires reasonable security practices to protect children's and teens' information. [S2]
Operators must notify a parent or teen before storing, transferring, or providing access to a child's or teen's personal information in a foreign adversary country listed as a 'covered nation.' [S2]

Larger platforms meeting a $3 billion revenue and 300 million monthly user threshold face a stricter 'knowledge' standard, where willfully ignoring evidence that a user is a minor counts as knowing, and the FTC must report annually on enforcement. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Social media platforms, app developers, and online advertising companies bear compliance costs and lose revenue from targeted advertising to minors. Smaller website and app operators also face new obligations, though the bill requires the FTC to analyze the impact of its rules on small businesses. [S2]

drawbacks.text: The bill includes a preemption clause barring states from maintaining or enforcing any law that relates to the Act's provisions, which could erase stronger state privacy protections for children and teens in favor of a single federal floor. [S2]
For operators that are not large platforms, the law only applies when they have 'actual knowledge' a user is a child or teen, leaving a gap for sites that avoid learning their users' ages. [S2]
The foreign-country provision requires notice to parents rather than prohibiting storage in adversary countries outright. [S2]

The bill lets education-technology vendors collect student data without parental consent under a written school agreement, provided the data is limited to educational purposes, which shifts consent decisions from families to school administrators. [S2]
Enforcement depends entirely on FTC resources; the bill directs the agency to report on its actions and investigations but adds no dedicated enforcement funding. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections are real and address a long-running problem: companies profiling children for advertising and holding their data indefinitely. The bill's design has weak points, especially the preemption of state laws, which supporters of stronger state protections have criticized, and the reliance on 'actual knowledge' for smaller operators. On balance the protections outweigh those drawbacks, but the preemption clause is a meaningful trade-off rather than a free win. [S2]

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared its House subcommittee 14-10 on December 11, 2025, and now waits for the full Energy and Commerce Committee to act; the House and Senate have not voted on it. [S4]

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Walberg introduced the bill on November 25, 2025, with Rep. Laurel Lee of Florida as a cosponsor, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce. [S1]
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade, which held a consideration and markup session on December 11, 2025. [S4]
The subcommittee forwarded the bill to the full committee by a vote of 14 to 10. [S4]

The bill text defines a 'high-impact social media company' as an operator with $3 billion or more in annual revenue and 300 million or more monthly active users, subjecting these largest platforms to a stricter standard for when they are deemed to know a user is a minor. [S2]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the ad-tech and social media industries are better off, because targeted advertising to children and teens remains legal while the bill sits one step short of the full committee. Children and teens gain nothing until the bill becomes law.

sides.party_line_note: The vote to advance the bill out of subcommittee was 14-10, but the record does not break the vote down by party; both of the bill's sponsors are Republicans. [S4]

industries.note: The bill outlaws building targeted ads around children's and teens' personal information, including demographic profiling, which removes a core way this industry monetizes young users. The advertising interest here runs directly against families' privacy. [S2]

The bill costs these platforms targeted-ad revenue and imposes a stricter knowledge standard for identifying minor users, but its preemption clause would also wipe out a patchwork of stronger state privacy laws in favor of one federal standard. [S2]

The bill lets operators collecting student data bypass parental consent by signing written agreements with schools that limit use to educational purposes, locking in their role in classrooms while easing their consent burden. [S2]

analysis.trajectory: The bill has cleared subcommittee and faces a full Energy and Commerce Committee markup next. Online child-safety bills have historically advanced when committee leadership schedules them together as a package, but with only one cosponsor and no Senate companion announced in this record, it could just as easily stall in committee the way many House privacy bills have.
